It has been said that "Āzar" was, among them, a term of blame in their language, as if [He said]: "And when Ibrāhīm said to his father: O you who err, do you take idols?"; if it is so, the choice is the nominative. It may also be a description of him, as if He said: "And when Ibrāhīm said to his father, the one who errs". It has also been said that "Āzar" is the name of an idol; if it is the name of an idol, its position is accusative on an implied verb, as if He said: "And when Ibrāhīm said to his father: Do you take Āzar as a god? Do you take idols as gods?".

zajjaj:75-75.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَكَذَلِكَ نُرِي إبْراهِيمَ مَلَكُوتَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾, i.e. and like what We have described of the story of Ibrāhīm — of what he said to his father — We show him the dominion (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth, i.e. the power by which his proof of the oneness of Allah, Majestic and Mighty, is strengthened. In speech you say to someone who has done you good or evil: «كذلك أجزيك» ("thus do I repay you"). The meaning of His words ﴿وَلِيَكُونَ مِنَ المُوقِنِينَ﴾ is: We show him the dominion of the heavens and the earth because of what he did, and so that he may remain firm in certainty.

«الملكوت» is like «الملك» (dominion), except that «الملكوت» is more intensive in the language than «الملك», because the wāw and the tāʾ are added for intensiveness (mubālagha). Like «الملكوت» are «الرغبوت» and «الرهبوت»; its pattern in terms of the verb is «فَعَلُوت». In the proverb: «رهبوتي خير من رغبوتي» ("being feared is better for me than being desired"), and this is like their saying «أو فرقًا خيرًا من حبّ» ("or fear [is] better than love"). Whoever relates it as «رهبوتي خير من رحموتي» ("being feared is better for me than being pitied"), it is a sound meaning: it establishes from the language that for one to have an awe by which one is feared is better than being pitied.
[Translator's note: «يحقق من اللسان» is as printed; its rendering here is tentative.]

zajjaj:76-76.t:
His words, Majestic and Mighty: ﴿فَلَمّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ رَأى كَوْكَبًا﴾: one says «جنّ عليه الليل» and «أجنّه الليل» when it becomes dark so that he is concealed by its darkness; and of everything that conceals one says «قد جنّ» and «قد أجنّ». One also says «جنّه الليل», but the choice is «جنّ عليه الليل» and «أجنّه الليل».

It has been said that the people of Ibrāhīm used to worship idols, the sun, the moon and the stars. When Ibrāhīm reached the stage at which reflection becomes obligatory and the proof becomes binding upon the servant, he looked into the things his people worshipped. When he saw the star which they worshipped, he said to them: ﴿هَذا رَبِّي﴾, i.e. according to your claim — as Allah, Majestic and Mighty, said: ﴿أيْنَ شُرَكائِيَ الَّذِينَ كُنْتُمْ تَزْعُمُونَ﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 62], attributing them to Himself in reporting their saying. ﴿فَلَمّا أفَلَ﴾, i.e. when it set; one says «أفل النجم يأفِل ويأفُل أفولًا» when it sets. ﴿قالَ لا أُحِبُّ الآفِلِينَ﴾, i.e. I do not love one whose state is that it rises and moves in a manner which makes clear that it is originated (muḥdath), moving from place to place, as all the other things do which you have agreed with me are not gods; i.e. I do not take as a god that whose state is this, just as you do not take as gods all the other things that are of this kind. It is not that he made his argument against them that whatever sets is not a god, because the heaven and the earth are visible, not absent, and this claim is not made about them; he only wanted to make clear to them what is near at hand, because its setting is the nearest thing by which they could be debated, in what was apparent to them — as he said: ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْتِي بِالشَّمْسِ مِنَ المَشْرِقِ فَأْتِ بِها مِنَ المَغْرِبِ﴾ [al-Baqara: 258].

It has also been said that he said this while reflecting for himself; on this view it is like His words: ﴿وَوَجَدَكَ ضالا فَهَدى﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 7]. But Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has told of Ibrāhīm in His words: ﴿إذْ جاءَ رَبَّهُ بِقَلْبٍ سَلِيمٍ﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 84], so there is no doubt that he was safe from doubt entering him concerning the matter of Allah; and Allah knows best.

It may also be on an implied «القول» (saying), as if He said: ﴿فَلَمّا جَنَّ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ رَأى كَوْكَبًا قالَ هَذا رَبِّي﴾, as if he said: "You say: This is my lord", i.e. "you are the ones saying: This is my lord" — as He, Majestic and Mighty, said: ﴿وَإذْ يَرْفَعُ إبْراهِيمُ القَواعِدَ مِنَ البَيْتِ وإسْماعِيلُ رَبَّنا تَقَبَّلْ مِنّا﴾ [al-Baqara: 127], the meaning being: "the two of them say: Accept from us". Allah knows best the reality of this. What I hold regarding this saying is that he said to them: "You say: This is my lord", i.e. this governs me — because, as is related, they were people of the stars (astrologers); so he argued against them that what you claim to be a governor shows in it only the trace of something governed, nothing else.

zajjaj:78-78.t:
His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿فَلَمّا رَأى الشَّمْسَ بازِغَةً﴾, and «فلما رأى القمر بازغًا»: one says «قد بزغ القمر» when it begins to rise, and likewise the sun. The argument regarding the sun and the moon is like the argument regarding the star.

Those who said that he said «هذا ربي» by way of conjecture and reflection argued from his words: ﴿لَئِنْ لَمْ يَهْدِنِي رَبِّي لأكُونَنَّ مِنَ القَوْمِ الضّالِّينَ﴾ [al-Anʿām: 77]. But this does not necessitate that, because the prophets ask Allah to keep them firm upon guidance, and they know that were it not for Allah's guidance they would not be guided; and Ibrāhīm says: ﴿واجْنُبْنِي وبَنِيَّ أنْ نَعْبُدَ الأصْنامَ﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 35].

zajjaj:79-79.t: And His words: ﴿إنِّي وجَّهْتُ وجْهِيَ لِلَّذِي فَطَرَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ حَنِيفًا﴾, i.e. inclining to Islam with an inclination from which there is no return. «الحنف» is for there to be an inclination in the foot, namely that the big toe of one foot inclines towards the big toe of the other foot, so that this foot turns towards that foot, and this is congenital. «الحنيف» is the one whose inclination to Islam is sound, firm in it. The meaning of ﴿وَجَّهْتُ وجْهِيَ﴾ is: I have made the aim of my worship my affirming the oneness of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

zajjaj:80-80.t: His words, Majestic and Exalted: ﴿وَحاجَّهُ قَوْمُهُ﴾: the meaning is: they disputed with him concerning Allah, so he said: ﴿أتُحاجُّونِّي في اللَّهِ﴾. Their disputing with him was — and Allah knows best — about what they worshipped alongside Allah, Mighty and Majestic, of the stars, the sun, the moon and the idols. So he said: ﴿أتُحاجُّونِّي في اللَّهِ﴾, i.e. concerning the oneness of Allah, ﴿وَقَدْ هَدانِي﴾, and He has made clear to me that by which I have been guided. ﴿وَلا أخافُ ما تُشْرِكُونَ بِهِ﴾, i.e. these things which you worship neither harm nor benefit, and I do not fear them. ﴿إلا أنْ يَشاءَ رَبِّي شَيْئًا﴾: unless He wills to punish me for a sin, if one should come from me. The position of «أن» is accusative, i.e. I fear nothing but the will of Allah.
